body.p: Greek has 24 letters. Most consonants sound as you expect; the surprises are **β** [v], **γ** (a throaty [ɣ], or [j] before e and i sounds), **δ** [ð] as in *this*, **θ** [θ] as in *think*, **χ** (like the *ch* in Scottish *loch*), **ρ** (tapped, as in Spanish).

body.tip: Sigma is written **ς** at the end of a word and **σ** everywhere else: **σεισμός** "earthquake". Η, Ι, Υ (and the pairs ΕΙ, ΟΙ, ΥΙ) all sound [i]; Ο and Ω both sound [o]. Spelling tells you about grammar and history, not sound.

solved.why: Use ς only at the very end of a word; the first two sigmas are inside the word.

solved.why: Before β, γ, δ, μ, ν, ρ the letter σ is voiced: κόσμος, Σμύρνη, σβήνω.

check.why: δ is the soft *th* of *this*; θ is the hard *th* of *think*.

check.why: Ο and ω are both [o].

check.why: ξ as in ξέρω "I know", ταξί "taxi".

sections.title: Letter pairs that make one sound

body.p: Some pairs of letters are read as a single sound. Learn this table and you can read anything.

**αυ** and **ευ** sound **af/ef** before the voiceless sounds θ, κ, ξ, π, σ, τ, φ, χ, ψ, and **av/ev** before vowels and all other consonants: **αυ**τός [af-], **αύ**ριο [av-], **ευ**χαριστώ [ef-], **Ευ**ρώπη [ev-].

A diaeresis (two dots, διαλυτικά) breaks a pair: **κορο**ϊ**δεύω** [ko-ro-i-] "I tease", **τσάι** [tsa-i] "tea" (here the stress mark already separates α and ι, so no dots are needed), **Μάιος** "May".

body.tip: In **μπ, ντ, γκ** the nasal (m, n, ng) is often barely heard in fast speech, even in the middle of a word: many speakers say [kodá] for κοντά. Both are correct.

solved.why: αυ/ευ = af/ef before voiceless τ, χ; av/ev before ρ and vowels.
μπ at the start = b, ντ at the start = d.

solved.q: Why does **τσάι** have no diaeresis but **κοροϊδεύω** does?
solved.a: In τσάι the stress mark on ά already shows that α and ι are separate
solved.why: The dots are needed only when the first vowel is unstressed: κορο-ϊ-δεύω, but τσά-ι, Μά-ι-ος.

check.why: αι = e: και [ke], είμαι [ime].
Before the voiceless χ, ευ = ef.
Before ρ, αυ = av.

check.why: μπ at the start = b; β is [v].

check.answer: ο and ι are read separately
check.why: Without the dots οι would be read [i].
ου = u (ουρανός, πού).

body.p: Every word of two or more syllables carries a stress mark (΄) on the stressed vowel: **ώρα, καφές, θάλασσα**. One-syllable words normally have none: **και, να, θα, το, μου**. The stress can fall only on one of the **last three** syllables.

The mark goes on the vowel, never on a consonant. On a pair it goes on the **second** letter: **είμαι, ούτε, αύριο, εύκολο** "easy". On a capital it goes before the letter: **Άννα, Έλα!** On words written all in capitals it is left out: **ΕΞΟΔΟΣ** "EXIT".
The stress changes meaning, so never leave it out:

body.tip: Exceptions with a stress mark on one syllable: **πού** and **πώς** (questions "where? how?") versus **που** and **πως** ("that, who" and "that"); **ή** "or" versus **η** "the"; and a weak pronoun after a stressed word that needs a second accent (see next section).

solved.why: On a vowel pair the mark goes on the second letter: ε**ύ**.

solved.why: The accent marks the question word, though both are one syllable.

check.why: On the pair ου the mark goes on υ.

sections.title: Stress that moves, and the double accent

body.p: When a word gets longer at the end, the stress may have to move forward to stay within the last three syllables:

ex.el: το τηλέφωνο → τα τηλέφωνα → των τηλεφώνων

body.p: The second rule is the **double accent**. A weak pronoun (μου, σου, του, της, το, μας, σας, τους...) after a word stressed on the third-last syllable makes four syllables after the stress, which Greek does not allow. So the word gets a second accent on its last syllable:
If the word is stressed on the second-last syllable, nothing changes: **το σπίτι μου, η μητέρα σου, Πες μου.**

solved.q: Put a weak pronoun after **το πρόσωπο** "face": "his face"
solved.why: πρόσωπο is stressed on the third-last syllable, so it takes a second accent before του.

solved.q: Make the genitive singular of **ο άνθρωπος**
solved.why: The ending -ου lengthens the word; the stress moves to the second-last syllable.

solved.q: Does **το όνομα** + **σου** take a second accent?
solved.why: ό-νο-μα is stressed on the third-last syllable.

solved.q: Does **η μητέρα** + **μου** take a second accent?
solved.why: μη-τέ-ρα is stressed on the second-last syllable.

check.why: τη-λέ-φω-νο + σου needs a second accent on the last syllable.
σπί-τι is stressed on the second-last syllable: no second accent.
The stress moves to the second-last syllable: τη-λε-φώ-νων.
Δι-ά-βα-σε is stressed on the third-last syllable, so it takes a second accent before το.
Third-last stress + μας: second accent on the last syllable.
αυ-το-κί-νη-το + μου: second accent on -τό.
Third-last stress: όνομά σου.
The stress moves forward when the ending grows.
Τη-λε-φώ-νη-σε is stressed on the third-last syllable: Τηλεφώνησέ μου.

body.p: The words **την, στην, τον, στον, δεν, μην** and **έναν** (and **αυτήν** in the accusative) can lose their final **-ν**. The rule for **τη(ν), στη(ν), δε(ν), μη(ν)**:

list: **Keep the ν** before a vowel and before **κ, π, τ, ξ, ψ, γκ, μπ, ντ, τσ, τζ**.
**Drop it** before all other consonants: β, γ, δ, ζ, θ, λ, μ, ν, ρ, σ, φ, χ.

ex.el: την Αθήνα, την κόρη, την πόρτα
τη Μαρία, τη θάλασσα, τη ζωή

ex.en: I don't know. / I don't want to.

body.p: The masculine **τον** and **στον** keep their **-ν** always in careful writing (**τον φίλο μου**), so you never confuse them with the neuter **το**. **Δεν** is so often written in full that **δεν θέλω** is also accepted; the official school grammar gives **δε θέλω**.

body.tip: A common slip: **τη μπλούζα** and **τη ντομάτα** look natural but are wrong. Before μπ and ντ keep the ν: **την μπλούζα**, **την ντομάτα**.

sections.title: The apostrophe and dropped vowels in speech

body.p: In everyday speech, when two vowels meet, one may drop. Writing shows it with an apostrophe (΄) where the vowel was lost:

Common fixed forms: **σ' αγαπώ**, **τ' όνομά σου**, **μ' αρέσει** (from **μου αρέσει** "I like it"), **απ' όλα** "of everything", **γι' αυτό** "that's why". **Γι'** before a vowel stands for **για**: **γι' αυτό, γι' εσένα**.
If the dropped vowel carried the stress, what is left is usually one syllable and takes no accent: **θα 'ρθω**, **μου 'πες** "you told me".

body.tip: These forms are informal but perfectly normal in messages, songs and dialogue. In formal writing prefer the full forms: **το έχω, θα έρθω, μου είπε**. Γι' αυτό and σ' αγαπώ are fine everywhere.

solved.q: Write the spoken form of **θα έρθω**
solved.why: The initial έ of έρθω drops; the apostrophe marks it.

solved.q: Write the full form of **γι' αυτό**
solved.why: γι' is the elided form of για before a vowel; γι' αυτό "that's why" is standard.

solved.q: Write the full form of **μ' αρέσει**
solved.why: In speech μου loses its vowel before α.

check.q: Which is the elided form of **σε αγαπώ**?
check.why: The ε of σε drops before the vowel α: σ' αγαπώ.
Γι' αυτό is the standard spelling.
The ει of είπε drops and the apostrophe goes before the remaining syllables.

check.q: Which is the full form of **τ' όνομά σου**?
check.why: The article το elides before ό; the double accent stays.
The dropped vowel is έ.
από loses its ο before ε.
The ο of το drops before έ.

title: Letters, sounds and stress
part: Μέρος Α΄ | Γράμματα και ήχοι | Letters and sounds
blurb: The 24 letters, the letter pairs that make one sound, where the stress falls and the spelling rules that change a word's look but not its sound.

intro.p: Greek spelling looks hard because one sound can be written several ways (the sound [i] has six spellings), but reading is easy: almost every letter or letter pair has one pronunciation. Learn the pairs once and you can read any sign, menu or text message aloud.

This chapter gives the sounds, the letter pairs, the rules of the stress mark (τόνος) and the small spelling changes you meet every day: the final -ν, the apostrophe, and the stress that moves when a word gets longer.
